analysis: Leander Allen Plummer II (1857-1914) is one of the very few artists in the whole sale where the antique line and the Maine connection genuinely coincide -- he died in 1914, so every work he made predates 1926 without argument. A New Bedford and Maine marine painter, so the subject matter is on-brief too. At $500-700 this is the best antique-plus-Maine picture inside the band.
problems: Only two photographs, which is thin. Plummer is a minor name with a shallow comparable record, so the estimate is the house's judgement. Establish medium and check for relining and overpaint in the sky, the usual failings in marine oils.
patience: Low to moderate. Artists who died before 1926 with a Maine association are genuinely scarce in this sale.

analysis: Frederick 'Ed' Ilsley (MA/ME, 1855-1933) at $600-800, with a second at 1203 for the same money. His working life straddles the antique line, so a mature work has a real chance of clearing 1926, and the Maine association is stated.
problems: Straddles rather than clears the line, so status is border until the picture itself is dated. Two lots means no scarcity -- compare both and bid the better. Minor name with a thin record.
patience: Moderate -- two chances in this sale.

analysis: The second Ilsley at $600-800 with four photographs -- slightly better documented than 1201.
problems: Same as 1201. Whichever of the two shows the better condition and the more saleable subject is the one to take.

analysis: Edward A. Page (MA, 1850-1928) at $500-700. Died in 1928, so the overwhelming majority of his output predates the antique line -- another of the handful of lots where age is close to settled rather than argued. A Massachusetts painter, so New England rather than Maine.
problems: Border rather than antique because two years of his output falls the wrong side. Minor name. Establish the medium and subject; a coastal New England subject strengthens the case locally.

analysis: Amanda Brewster Sewell (1859-1926) at $400-600 -- she died in the antique-line year itself, so effectively all her work qualifies. Sewell was a properly trained academic painter who exhibited at the 1893 Chicago Exposition, and women painters of that generation have been steadily reassessed upward.
problems: Five photographs, which is decent. Her market remains thin despite the reassessment, so do not expect resale strength. Check for relining and for the darkened varnish typical of academic oils of the period.
patience: Moderate. Turn-of-the-century American women painters at this money are consistently undervalued.

analysis: Horace Bonham (PA, 1835-1892) at $500-700. Died in 1892, so this is unambiguously antique -- one of very few lots in the sale where the dating needs no argument at all. Bonham is best known for genre scenes of cockfight spectators and has a small but real collector base.
problems: Pennsylvania rather than Maine, so this rests on the antique and named-maker criteria. Four photographs. Nineteenth-century American genre painting is a soft market; buy on the age and the quality, not on appreciation.
patience: Moderate. Genuinely pre-1900 signed American oils inside this band are not common.

analysis: Carl Gustaf Simon Nelson (MA/ME/SWEDEN, 1898-1988) at $800-1,200. A Maine association is stated and he was a competent modernist painter with a modest following.
problems: Only just inside the band. Triple-state attribution, so the Maine claim is one of three. Long career means deep supply. Establish medium and subject.

analysis: Howard Hall Darnell (PA/ME, 1858-1939) at $1,000-1,500 -- and Day 2 offers three more Darnells at 2267, 2269 and 2270, all at the same estimate. Four lots by one artist across two days is a consignment. His working life straddles the antique line.
problems: Out of band at $1,000-1,500, and with four lots in the sale there is no scarcity argument whatsoever. If any of the four stalled near the ceiling it would be worth a look; otherwise let them go.
patience: Not applicable -- out of band, and four chances means the market will find its level.

analysis: Iona McKinney (ME, 1899-2006) at $300-500 -- a Maine artist at the cheap end, and a 107-year life means a long working span. One of the sub-$500 Maine lots where this budget actually buys something.
problems: Minor regional name with almost no market record. Three photographs. Establish medium and subject; a recognisable Maine coastal view is worth materially more locally than a still life.

analysis: Louis Doyle Norton (ME/NH, 1868-1940) at $400-600. Working life straddles the antique line, Maine association stated, and the price is inside the band -- a reasonable combination of two criteria at low cost.
problems: Border on age until the picture is dated. Minor name, three photographs. Look for a date on the canvas.

analysis: Frank Handlen (ME, 1916-2023) at $300-400. A long-lived Maine artist -- he worked into his hundreds -- and at this price one of the cheapest Maine lots in Day 1.
problems: Very long career means substantial supply, and he died recently so estate material may continue to appear. Three photographs. Establish medium.

analysis: Parker S. Perkins (Rockport, MA, 1862-1942) at $400-600. A Cape Ann painter -- the Rockport colony rather than Maine, but the same coastal New England idiom and the working life straddles the antique line.
problems: Not Maine, so this rests on named maker and possible antique status. Rockport painters are abundant and the market is well supplied. Four photographs.
patience: High. Cape Ann material runs constantly in New England sales.

analysis: Anthony Thieme (MA/CA, 1888-1954) at $300-400, with a second at 1474 for the same money. Thieme was a genuinely successful Rockport painter whose harbour scenes sell well -- so two at $300-400 is either a bargain or, more likely, they are prints or minor works rather than the harbour oils that make thousands.
problems: Establish what these actually are. A Thieme oil does not sell for $300; if these are oils, expect condition problems or a very small size. Three photographs each. Treat a suspiciously cheap good name as a red flag first.

analysis: The second Anthony Thieme at $300-400. Same question as 1461 -- why is a saleable Rockport name this cheap?
problems: Same as 1461. Compare both at preview; if they are genuine small oils in sound condition, either is a good buy at $300.

analysis: Three 1940s sketchbooks by Denny Sonke Winters at $600-800. Sketchbooks are a different and more interesting proposition than a finished picture: they are unique, they show the artist working, and three of them from a dated decade is a coherent archive. Winters was a serious painter with a Maine association, and Day 3 offers two of her finished works at 3465 and 3466.
problems: Sketchbooks have a narrower audience than paintings -- they appeal to researchers and completists rather than decorators, which caps resale. Check how full they are and whether the bindings are sound. Three photographs for three books is thin.
patience: Low to moderate. Artist sketchbooks are genuinely uncommon and cannot be replaced.

analysis: Stow Wengenroth, 'The Sloop', at $600-800 -- one of the nine consecutive Wengenroth lithographs (1308-1316) I have rated as a block. Wengenroth is the finest American black-and-white lithographer of the century and the only printmaker here whose Maine subjects are collected outside the state. A sloop is a strong marine subject.
problems: Only one photograph, so condition is unknown -- and mid-century lithographs that hung in Maine cottages are routinely light-stained and mat-burned. Check for a pencil signature below the image. Nine in one sale means real bidder exhaustion by the end; be patient and take whichever falls.
patience: Moderate to high -- nine chances in one afternoon.

analysis: Wengenroth, 'The Little Fellows', at $600-800. An animal or bird subject rather than a coastal one, which makes it less on-brief and therefore more likely to go cheap -- often the best reason to bid.
problems: One photograph. Non-coastal subjects have a smaller audience, which is the opportunity and also the resale limitation.

analysis: Wengenroth, 'Island Home', 1968 -- one of only three in the run with a stated date, which makes it better documented than its siblings. An island house is a strongly Maine subject.
problems: One photograph. A dated late work; Wengenroth's editions of the 1960s are as large as his earlier ones, so the date adds documentation rather than rarity.

analysis: Wengenroth, 'Windy Shore'. A coastal subject, so on-brief within the block.
problems: One photograph, condition unknown. Same block strategy applies.

analysis: Wengenroth, 'Along the Shore', 1938 -- the earliest dated lithograph in the run. His 1930s work is generally the most sought after, so of the nine this is the one I would rank highest on paper.
problems: One photograph, and a 1938 sheet has had nearly ninety years to acquire foxing and light-staining. Check the margins and look for the pencil signature.
patience: Moderate. The early dated impressions are the desirable end of his output.

analysis: Wengenroth, 'Tide Pool'. Coastal subject, undated.
problems: One photograph. Same as the rest of the block.

analysis: Wengenroth, 'The Fog Bell', 1954. A dated mid-career sheet with a strongly Maine coastal subject -- a fog bell is about as regionally specific as his imagery gets.
problems: One photograph. Being second-to-last in the nine-lot run is a good position for a cheap purchase.

analysis: John French Sloan (1871-1951) at $500-700. Sloan is a major figure -- an Eight, an Armory Show organiser, in every American museum -- so a $500 estimate means this is an etching rather than a painting. Sloan's etchings are genuine, properly catalogued works with a real market, and they are the only way his name enters this budget.
problems: Establish that it is a lifetime impression rather than a posthumous restrike, and check for a pencil signature. Sloan's plates were reprinted, and unsigned later impressions are worth a fraction. Note that his wife Helen Farr Sloan appears at 1331 in the same sale, which suggests a related consignment.
patience: Moderate. Sloan etchings appear regularly and are consistently affordable relative to his standing.

analysis: Helen Farr Sloan (1911-2005) at $400-600 -- John Sloan's second wife, herself a painter and the person most responsible for his posthumous reputation and the Delaware Art Museum holdings. Her presence alongside lot 1009 confirms a Sloan-related consignment.
problems: Her market is far smaller than her historical importance; she is collected as an adjunct to Sloan rather than in her own right. Four photographs. Establish medium.

analysis: Raphael Soyer (1889-1987) at $600-800. Another major American name -- a leading Social Realist with deep museum representation -- so again the price tells you this is a print or a drawing rather than a canvas. Soyer's lithographs and etchings are legitimate and collected.
problems: Establish the medium, edition and signature. Soyer was prolific in print and his editions are not scarce. Note his brother Moses Soyer appears at 3109 in Day 3, so the two consignments may be related.

analysis: Lynd Ward (1905-1985) at $600-800, with a second at 1176 for the same money. Ward was the master of the American wood engraving and effectively invented the wordless novel -- his blocks are technically extraordinary and he is properly collected. Works on paper by a serious name inside the band, which is the pattern the brief identifies as good value.
problems: Establish whether this is an original wood engraving or a book illustration plate -- the gap is large, and Ward's images circulate heavily as reproductions from his novels. Look for a pencil signature and for the crisp relief bite of a genuine engraving.

analysis: The second Lynd Ward at $600-800. Same reasoning as 1099.
problems: Same medium question. Bid whichever of the two proves to be an original engraving.

analysis: Louis John Rhead (1857-1926) at $1,000-1,500 -- the companion to lot 1332 at the same estimate. Rhead is one of the genuinely few authentic Art Nouveau practitioners in this sale, an Anglo-American poster designer working in the full Continental idiom, and he died in 1926 so the work is antique-eligible. This is a real criterion-three hit.
problems: Out of band at $1,000-1,500 with a $500 opening -- both Rhead lots start above the ceiling, which is frustrating given how well they fit. Six photographs here. If either stalled near $900 it would justify a stretch on criteria grounds; establish first whether these are period stone lithographs or 1970s poster-revival reprints.
patience: Low. Genuine period Nouveau posters are exactly what this buyer says they want and they do not appear often at Thomaston.

analysis: Norman Rockwell at $1,000-1,500, the first of four Rockwell lots (1211, 1213, 1215, 1217). Rockwell originals are seven-figure objects, so these are prints -- and the Rockwell print market is one of the most thoroughly muddied there is, with authorised signed collotypes and lithographs sitting alongside vast quantities of unsigned reproductions and outright fakes.
problems: Out of band anyway, but the substantive warning is the same as the Wyeth blocks: no process, no edition, no publisher stated on any of the four. Rockwell's signature was also extensively forged on reproductions in the 1970s and 80s. Treat a cheap famous name as a red flag first.
patience: Not applicable -- out of band, and Rockwell reproductions are endless.

analysis: Second Rockwell at $1,000-1,500, process unstated.
problems: Out of band. Same as 1211.

analysis: Third Rockwell at $1,000-1,500, process unstated.
problems: Out of band.

analysis: The cheapest Rockwell at $400-600 -- inside the band, and the only one of the four that is. Being the cheap one in a run of four by a famous name is exactly where an unsigned open-edition reproduction sits.
problems: In band but almost certainly a reproduction. Four photographs, so look for a pencil signature, an edition number and a publisher's blindstamp. Absent all three, this is a $100 decorative print regardless of the estimate.

analysis: Andrew Wyeth at $400-600 -- the first of the Day 1 Wyeth material, running 1158-1161 and 1172 before the named-process block at 1163-1171. Lot 1164 in that block has been proved a 1993 Aaron Ashley commercial reproduction, which sets the standard for the whole consignment.
problems: No process, no edition, no date stated. Inside the band, but a reproduction at $400 is a bad buy at any budget. Establish process and signature or assume the worst.
patience: Irrelevant -- Wyeth reproductions are continuously available.

analysis: Wyeth at $300-400, process unstated.
problems: Same as 1158.

analysis: Wyeth at $300-400 with six photographs -- the best-documented of this sub-group, so the one where the margin inscriptions can actually be read.
problems: Six photographs is an opportunity: look for a printed copyright line or publisher's mark of the kind that condemned 1164. Same assumption otherwise.

analysis: Wyeth at $200-300 with a single photograph -- the cheapest Wyeth in Day 1.
problems: One photograph and no process. Nothing here can be assessed without seeing the sheet.

analysis: Wyeth at $300-500, immediately after the named-process block -- so the cataloguer had just finished describing giclees and portfolios and reverted to no description at all.
problems: That reversion is itself informative. Four photographs. Same assumption.

analysis: The first of a second Day 1 Wyeth run -- ten consecutive lots, 1431-1440, all at $200-300 with $50 openings and one or two photographs each. Ten identically priced Wyeths from one consignor is as clear a signal of mass-produced reproductions as this sale offers.
problems: None of the ten names a process. The uniform $200-300 estimate across ten lots tells you the house is pricing them as decorative prints, whatever the room does with the name.

analysis: Second of the ten-lot Wyeth run at $200-300.
problems: Same as 1431.

analysis: Third of the run at $200-300.
problems: Same as 1431.

analysis: Fourth of the run at $200-300.
problems: Same as 1431.

analysis: Fifth of the run at $200-300.
problems: Same as 1431.

analysis: Sixth of the run at $200-300.
problems: Same as 1431.

analysis: Seventh of the run at $200-300.
problems: Same as 1431.

analysis: Eighth of the run at $200-300.
problems: Same as 1431.

analysis: Ninth of the run at $200-300.
problems: Same as 1431.

analysis: Last of the ten-lot Wyeth run at $200-300. Twenty-six Wyeth lots across Day 1 in total, plus eleven more in Day 3 -- thirty-seven in one sale.
problems: Thirty-seven Wyeth lots is not a coincidence; it is a consignment strategy built on the most famous name in Maine painting. None of the thirty-seven names a process except the giclee at 1163 and the proved reproduction at 1164.

analysis: 'AFTER Pablo Picasso' at $500-700. The catalogue commits honestly here, and per the standing principles 'after' means copy or reproduction. This is useful as a calibration point: it shows how the house describes this material when it does commit, which throws the bare 'PABLO PICASSO' entries at 1467, 1468 and 1469 into relief.
problems: Six photographs. A reproduction after Picasso is a decorative object; $500-700 is an optimistic estimate for one.

analysis: Picasso at $300-400, the second of three consecutive lots catalogued with only his name and dates. Compare directly with 1150, which the same cataloguer marked 'after Picasso' -- the difference in labelling is not matched by a difference in price, which suggests these three are the same class of object.
problems: Nothing genuine by Picasso lands at $300. These will be later lithographic reproductions, Verve or Cahiers d'Art plates, or unsigned exhibition material. Three photographs.

analysis: Third Picasso at $300-400.
problems: Same as 1468.

analysis: 'AFTER Jean-Jacques Henner' at $500-700. Henner's languid redheads were among the most copied academic images of the late 19th century, and the catalogue is explicit that this is a copy.
problems: 'After' is disqualifying on authenticity. Academic copies of this kind were painted in quantity as decorative work; the estimate is well above what one supports.

analysis: A portrait of an American boy, circa 1900, at $600-800. Catalogued to a date, anonymous so no maker premium, and right on the antique line.
problems: The brief names anonymous 19th-century child portraits specifically as a weak market, and this is that category one decade later. Charming on a wall, hard to resell. Three photographs -- check for relining and overcleaning in the face, where damage matters most.
patience: Very high. Anonymous child portraits run at every sale and routinely fail to sell.

analysis: A 19th-century Boston School portrait of a child at $700-900. Catalogued to the century, so genuinely antique, and 'Boston School' places it in a recognised tradition.
problems: Per the standing principles, 'School' with no name attached is a hopeful label rather than an attribution -- price it as the anonymous work it is. And again this is the weak-market child-portrait category. Four photographs.

analysis: A Hudson Valley 'style' landscape, unsigned, at $500-700. The catalogue's word is 'style', which per the standing principles means the cataloguer is declining to commit to a period -- so this is not being offered as a Hudson River School picture.
problems: 'Style' plus 'unsigned' means no attribution and no date. Hudson River School imagery was painted as decoration well into the 20th century. Check the canvas, stretcher and craquelure before assuming any age.

analysis: An American still life of fish, unframed, at $300-400. Fish still lifes are a distinct 19th-century American genre with a small dedicated following, and unframed means you see the whole canvas including the edges -- useful for judging age.
problems: No date and no artist. Unframed also means framing cost on top. Three photographs. Look at the tacking edges and stretcher for genuine period construction.

analysis: A 19th-century mountain landscape initialled 'WGS' at $300-400. Catalogued to the century so genuinely antique, and cheap.
problems: Initials are not an attribution -- per the standing principles an unidentified signature is speculative, so price this as anonymous period landscape. Four photographs.

analysis: A Mabel Copeland floral, circa 1900, at $500-700, with a companion at 1401. Catalogued to a date on the antique line and a named if obscure artist.
problems: Copeland has essentially no market record, so the name adds nothing. Floral still lifes of this period are abundant. Two lots means no scarcity.

analysis: The second Mabel Copeland floral at $500-700.
problems: Same as 1399. Bid whichever is in better condition.

analysis: A harbour scene with docked boats, unknown artist, 20th century, oil on linen, at $300-400. Catalogued honestly as 20th century and anonymous -- so no false claims, and a harbour scene is decoratively useful in a Maine house.
problems: Explicitly 20th century, so no antique claim, and anonymous, so no maker interest. This is a decorating purchase. Four photographs.

analysis: Cornelia Cowles Vetter (1880-1957), harbour scene, at $300-500. A named artist with dates, a marine subject, and a working life that straddles the antique line.
problems: Minor name with a thin record. Four photographs. Establish medium and whether the harbour is identifiable -- a named New England port would strengthen it locally.

analysis: Mary Herrick Fenner of Millbury, Massachusetts, oil on panel, at $300-500. A named artist tied to a named town, and oil on panel rather than canvas, which often indicates an earlier date.
problems: No dates given for the artist at all, so the period is unverified. Fenner has no market record to speak of. Three photographs. Panel can split -- check the reverse.

analysis: 'Lovely Young Lady with Brunette Hair in finger curls, ruffled lacy decolletage, her eyes downcast demurely, OIL ON IVORY, signed lower right. In gilt cast brass oval frame.' A pretty and competent miniature, and the support is elephant ivory. Federal ESA rules do allow a narrow de minimis exemption for a small, fixed, pre-1975 ivory component, and a painted wafer is a far better candidate for it than a solid carved figure -- but the exemption needs documentation of age and origin that this lot does not supply, and state law varies on top of it. Resale is recorded as zero on that basis, consistent with lot 2342. Paperwork could restore it; nothing in the catalogue is paperwork.
problems: Elephant ivory support, undocumented, so resale is zero. E. Wenzel is also an unindexed signature -- the standing principle applies and there is no maker premium to be had here even setting the material aside.

analysis: An unsigned French watercolour genre scene at $500-700. Anonymous, so no maker premium to pay.
problems: No date at all, only two photographs, and 'French genre scene' covers an enormous range of quality and period. Watercolour fading is the standard risk.

analysis: A nude signed 'F.L., 95' at $300-500. The interesting question is which 95 -- 1895 or 1995 -- and the catalogue does not say, which is a hundred-year ambiguity in a two-digit date.
problems: Unidentified initials and an ambiguous date. Four photographs. The paint surface and support will settle the century immediately at preview; until then this could be a Victorian academic study or a 1990s life-class exercise.

analysis: A small genre painting of a child playing at $250-350. Cheap, small, and anonymous.
problems: No date, no artist, and it sits in the weak child-subject category. Three photographs. Purely a decorating purchase.

analysis: An Art Deco gouache of birds by Adams at $300-400. Genuine period Deco design work on paper, if the dating holds, and decorative bird subjects of the 1920s and 30s have a following.
problems: 'By Adams' is a surname with nothing attached -- an unidentified signature. Two photographs only. Gouache is prone to flaking and to fading. Establish the period from the paper and the framing.

analysis: An American Western subject painting, 1930s, at $300-400. Catalogued to a decade and anonymous.
problems: Wrong region entirely for this brief, and 1930s Western imagery was produced in quantity as commercial illustration. Four photographs.

analysis: A 1995 Russian self-portrait at $300-400. Dated to the year and thirty years old -- modern by any reading.
problems: No criteria fit whatsoever: not antique, not Maine, no precious metal, no established maker. Five photographs. Post-Soviet paintings were exported in large numbers in the 1990s and have almost no US market.

analysis: Joel Janowitz (NY, 1945- ) at $500-1,000. A contemporary painter with genuine gallery and museum presence in the Boston area.
problems: The $500-1,000 estimate spread is unusually wide, which signals the house is unsure. Living artist, no criteria fit beyond the name. Five photographs.

analysis: John Manship at $800-1,200 with a marine subject. Manship was the son of the sculptor Paul Manship and a Gloucester painter.
problems: Note the catalogue gives his dates as '1977-2000', which would make him twenty-three at death and is almost certainly wrong -- John Manship lived 1927-2000. Another cataloguing error of the kind that recurs through this sale. Only just inside the band.
